rationale: The concurring justices cite this case as comparative authority supporting their point that consumer interests must be considered in determining just and reasonable rates, not just investor interests.

rationale: The concurring justices cite Justice Holmes' dissent in Baldwin v. Missouri to support their criticism of the Court's broad use of due process to invalidate legislation based on judges' views of reasonableness.

targetName: C & A Carbone, Inc. v. Town of Clarkstown

targetName: Vance v. W. A. Vandercook Co.

rationale: The Court cites Vance as historical precedent that upheld a state monopoly system, using it to support the argument that public entities can be treated differently than private ones under Commerce Clause analysis.

targetName: Dean Milk Co. v. City of Madison

rationale: The Court cites Granholm to help explain the holding in Scott v. Donald, using it to clarify that Scott involved discrimination in favor of in-state businesses rather than public entities.

quote: The Counties' flow control ordinances are properly analyzed under the test set forth in Pike v. Bruce Church, Inc., 397 U. S. 137, 142 (1970), which is reserved for laws 'directed to legitimate local concerns, with effects upon interstate commerce that are only incidental.'
rationale: The Court cites Pike as providing the appropriate test for analyzing laws that are directed at legitimate local concerns with only incidental effects on interstate commerce, applying this standard to the flow control ordinances.

quote: There was a time when this Court presumed to make such binding judgments for society, under the guise of interpreting the Due Process Clause. See Lochner v. New York, 198 U. S. 45 (1905). rationale: The Court criticizes Lochner as representing an era of inappropriate judicial overreach, warning against similar judicial interference with state economic legislation under the dormant Commerce Clause.

targetName: City of Philadelphia v. New Jersey
quote: Discriminatory laws motivated by 'simple economic protectionism' are subject to a 'virtually per se rule of invalidity,' Philadelphia v. New Jersey, 437 U. S. 617, 624 (1978), which can only be overcome by a showing that the State has no other means to advance a legitimate local purpose.
rationale: The Court cites Philadelphia v. New Jersey to explain the standard for reviewing discriminatory laws motivated by economic protectionism, but distinguishes the present case as not falling into that category.

quote: 'Conceptually, of course, any notion of discrimination assumes a comparison of substantially similar entities.' General Motors Corp. v. Tracy, 519 U. S. 278, 298 (1997) (footnote omitted). But States and municipalities are not private businesses — far from it.

quote: Scott struck down two laws that discriminated in favor of in-state businesses and against out-of-state businesses; neither law favored local government at the expense of all private industry.
rationale: The Court cites Scott to clarify that it involved discrimination favoring in-state businesses rather than public entities, distinguishing it from the present case where the favored entity is a public corporation.

targetName: Oregon Waste Systems, Inc. v. Department of Environmental Quality of Ore.

rationale: The Court cites Oregon Waste Systems to define discrimination in the Commerce Clause context, but ultimately distinguishes the present case as not involving discrimination between in-state and out-of-state economic interests.

quote: 'The Commerce Clause significantly limits the ability of States and localities to regulate or otherwise burden the flow of interstate commerce, but it does not elevate free trade above all other values.' Maine v. Taylor, 477 U. S., at 151.
rationale: The Court cites Maine v. Taylor to support its position that the Commerce Clause does not automatically prioritize free trade over other legitimate state interests, such as the Counties' waste management policies.

targetName: Tyler Pipe Industries, Inc. v. Washington State Department of Revenue

targetName: West Lynn Creamery, Inc. v. Healy

targetName: Camps Newfound/Owatonna, Inc. v. Town of Harrison

rationale: The Court distinguishes Hughes and other market participant cases from the dormant Commerce Clause context, explaining that they are not applicable to sovereign immunity analysis.

rationale: The Court cites King positively as establishing that waivers of federal sovereign immunity cannot be implied but must be unequivocally expressed.

rationale: The Court cites Johnson positively as providing the classic definition of an effective waiver of a constitutional right.

targetName: Aetna Insurance v. Kennedy Ex Rel. Bogash

targetName: K Mart Corp. v. Cartier, Inc.
quote: See, e. g., K mart Corp. v. Cartier, Inc., 486 U. S. 176, 185-186 (1988) ('Trademark law, like contract law, confers private rights, which are themselves rights of exclusion. It grants the trademark owner a bundle of such rights').

targetName: Deitrick v. Standard Surety & Casualty Co.

quote: Iglehart v. Todd, 203 Ind. 427 ; 178 N. E. 685

targetName: Mount Vernon Trust Co. v. Bergoff

quote: Denny v. Fishter, 238 Ky. 127 ; 36 S. W. 2d 864
rationale: The court cites Denny v. Fishter as supporting the principle that one cannot rely on an illegal agreement to defeat the obligation of a note when the statute aims to protect creditors.

quote: In both capital and noncapital cases this Court has recognized that the decision in Weems v. United States 'proscribes punishment grossly disproportionate to the severity of the crime.' Ingraham v. Wright, 430 U. S. 651, 667 (1977)

quote: It is a matter of common knowledge that prosecutors often exercise their discretion in invoking recidivist statutes or in plea bargaining so as to screen out truly 'petty' offenders who fall within the literal terms of such statutes. rationale: The Court cites Oyler to support its position that prosecutorial discretion is a legitimate aspect of recidivist statutes, noting that such discretion can screen out truly petty offenders despite the literal terms of the statutes.

quote: In re Kemmler, 136 U. S. 436 (1890), provided the Court with its second opportunity to review methods of carrying out a death penalty. That case involved a constitutional challenge to New York's use of electrocution.
rationale: The Court cites Kemmler as an early case addressing methods of execution rather than proportionality of sentences, establishing historical context for Eighth Amendment jurisprudence, though this appears in Justice Powell's dissent.

quote: In both capital and noncapital cases this Court has recognized that the decision in Weems v. United States 'proscribes punishment grossly disproportionate to the severity of the crime.' Ingraham v. Wright, 430 U. S. 651, 667 (1977); see Hutto v. Finney, 437 U. S. 678, 685 (1978)

rationale: The Court cites Morrissey to support its consideration of parole as a relevant factor in assessing Rummel's sentence, noting that parole is an established variation on imprisonment that affects the actual time served.

quote: As Mr. Justice Holmes noted in his dissenting opinion in Lochner v. New York, 198 U. S. 45, 76 (1905), our Constitution 'is made for people of fundamentally differing views...'

quote: As Mr. Justice Frankfurter noted for the Court in Gore v. United States, 357 U. S. 386, 393 (1958), '[w]hatever views may be entertained regarding severity of punishment, whether one believes in its efficacy or its futility, . . . these are peculiarly questions of legislative policy.'
rationale: The Court cites Gore to support its position that questions about severity of punishment are primarily matters of legislative policy rather than judicial review, reinforcing the Court's deference to legislative judgment.

quote: The Court repeatedly has recognized that § 1983 embodies a strong congressional policy in favor of federal courts' acting as the primary and final arbiters of constitutional rights. quote: Stone v. Powell does not provide a logical doctrinal source for the court's ruling. This Court in Stone assessed the costs and benefits of the judge-made exclusionary rule within the boundaries of the federal courts' statutory power to issue writs of habeas corpus.

targetName: England v. Louisiana State Board of Medical Examiners
quote: The England decision is inapposite to the question before us. In the England case, a party first submitted to a federal court his claim that a state statute violated his constitutional rights. The federal court abstained and remitted the plaintiff to the state courts...

quote: Under collateral estoppel, once a court has decided an issue of fact or law necessary to its judgment, that decision may preclude relitigation of the issue in a suit on a different cause of action involving a party to the first case. Montana v. United States, 440 U. S. 147, 153.

quote: But in Preiser v. Rodriguez, 411 U. S. 475, 497, the Court noted with implicit approval the view of other federal courts that res judicata principles fully apply to civil rights suits brought under that statute.

targetName: Blonder-Tongue Laboratories, Inc. v. University of Illinois Foundation

targetName: Monell v. New York City Dept. of Social Servs.

quote: See also Huffman v. Pursue, Ltd., 420 U. S. 592, 606, n. 18; Wolff v. McDonnell, 418 U. S. 539, 554, n. 12.
rationale: The Court cites Wolff v. McDonnell in a string citation as supporting the application of res judicata principles to §1983 actions. The citation is used to establish precedent without any negative treatment.

quote: See, e. g., Maine v. Thiboutot, 448 U. S. 1 (1980); Monett v. New York City Dept. of Social Services, 436 U. S. 658 (1978); Imbler v. Pachtman, 424 U. S. 409 (1976).
rationale: The dissent cites Imbler v. Pachtman in a string citation as an example of the Court considering legislative intent when applying common-law doctrines to §1983. The citation acknowledges Imbler's authority without any negative treatment.

quote: Thus, res judicata and collateral estoppel not only reduce unnecessary litigation and foster reliance on adjudication, but also promote the comity between state and federal courts that has been recognized as a bulwark of the federal system. See Younger v. Harris, 401 U. S. 37, 43-45.

quote: Reliance is placed upon Deitrick v. Greaney, 309 U. S. 190. But that case rested on a plain violation of an explicit provision of a federal statute in force at the time of its occurrence. This is not true here.

quote: Were this Court, in the absence of federal legislation, to make its own choice of law, compare United States v. Guaranty Trust Co., 293 U. S. 340; O'Brien v. rationale: The opinion cites Erie as a reference point for when the decision was made, without criticizing or limiting it. The citation is neutral and informational.

rationale: The Court acknowledges Lincoln Mills as a valid example of when federal common law may properly fill gaps in a statute, without any negative treatment.

Although the Court has formulated 'interstate common law,' Kansas v. Colorado, 206 U. S. 46, 98 (1907), it has done so not because the usual separation-of-powers principles do not apply, but rather because interstate disputes frequently call for the application of a federal rule when Congress has not spoken.
rationale: The Court cites Kansas v. Colorado as an example of the Court formulating interstate common law, acknowledging its validity in appropriate circumstances without criticism.

targetName: The State of Texas v. Reuben Pankey

rationale: The Court limits the applicability of Wells by clarifying that it applies only in specific circumstances where the railroad does minimal business in the forum state.

targetName: New York, Chicago & St. Louis Rd. Co. v. Matzinger

rationale: The Court cites Terte to support its position that inconvenience of distant litigation is not sufficient grounds to restrict venue when the carrier operates in that jurisdiction.

quote: It is clear that the allowance or denial of this federal privilege is a matter of federal law, not a matter of state law under Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins, 304 U. S. 64, 72.
rationale: The Court cites Erie to clarify that the interpretation of federal venue provisions is a matter of federal law, not state law.

targetName: Government & Civic Employees Organizing Committee v. Windsor

targetName: National Ass'n for the Advancement of Colored People v. Button

rationale: The Court cites Button as supporting authority for the principle that parties have the right to return to federal court after state court proceedings in abstention cases, showing respect for the precedent.

quote: Since Erie R. Co. v. Tompkins, 304 U. S. 64, the federal courts under that head of jurisdiction daily have the task of determining what the state law is.

targetName: Louisiana Power & Light Co. v. City of Thibodaux

targetName: Harrison v. National Ass'n for the Advancement of Colored People

targetName: Lassiter v. Northampton County Board of Elections

rationale: The Court cites Lassiter as an example of a case where direct Supreme Court review followed state court proceedings. The citation is neutral and acknowledges the continuing validity of the precedent.

quote: The fact that those questions are complex and difficult is no excuse for a refusal by the District Court to entertain the suit. Meredith v. Winter Haven, 320 U. S. 228.

targetName: County of Allegheny v. Frank Mashuda Co.

quote: Our starting point must be the policy of federal jurisdiction which Erie R. Co. v. Tompkins, 304 U.S. 64, embodies. In overruling Swift v. Tyson, 16 Pet. 1, Erie R. Co. v. Tompkins did not merely overrule a venerable case.
rationale: The Court uses Erie as a foundational precedent for its analysis, building upon its principles rather than criticizing or limiting it. The opinion treats Erie as establishing an important policy regarding federal jurisdiction.

quote: In overruling Swift v. Tyson, 16 Pet. 1, Erie R. Co. v. Tompkins did not merely overrule a venerable case. It overruled a particular way of looking at law which dominated the judicial process long after its inadequacies had been laid bare.

Dow, supra, where the plaintiff in error had been convicted in a state court of a felony upon an information, and by a jury of eight persons, it was held that the indictment, made indispensable by the Fifth Amendment, and the trial by jury guaranteed by the Sixth Amendment, were not privileges and immunities of citizens of the United States, as those words were used in the Fourteenth Amendment.
rationale: The court cites Maxwell v. Dow as a key precedent establishing that Fifth and Sixth Amendment rights are not privileges and immunities of citizens protected against state action by the Fourteenth Amendment. The citation is central to the court's analysis.

quote: Since then all the States of the Union have, from time to time, with varying form but uniform meaning, included the privilege, in their constitutions, except the States of New Jersey and Iowa, and in those States it is held to be part of the existing law. State v. Zdanowicz, supra; State v. Height, 117 Iowa, 650.
rationale: The court cites State v. Height as establishing that in Iowa, despite not having a constitutional provision against self-incrimination, the privilege is recognized as part of existing law. The citation supports the court's historical analysis of the privilege.

targetName: Butchers' Benevolent Ass'n v. Crescent City Live-Stock Landing & Slaughter-House Co.
quote: The meaning of the phrase 'privileges and immunities of citizens of the United States,' as used in the Fourteenth Amendment, came under early consideration in the Slaughter-House Cases, 16 Wall. 36.
rationale: The court cites the Slaughter-House Cases as the foundational precedent for interpreting the privileges and immunities clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The citation is central to the court's analysis of the scope of that clause.

quote: Indeed, this court has not hesitated thus to characterize the Star Chamber method of compelling an accused to be a witness against himself. In Boyd v. United States, 116 U. S. 616, 631, 633, will be found some weighty observations by Mr. Justice Bradley, delivering the judgment of the court, as to the scope and meaning of the Fourth and Fifth Amendments.
rationale: Justice Harlan in his dissent cites Boyd v. United States as containing important observations about the Fourth and Fifth Amendments. The majority opinion does not directly cite or criticize Boyd, so the treatment is based on the dissent's positive reference.

quote: These observations were referred to approvingly in Counselman v. Hitchcock, 142 U. S. 547, 580, 581.
rationale: Justice Harlan in his dissent notes that Counselman v. Hitchcock approvingly referenced the observations in Boyd v. United States. The majority opinion does not directly cite or criticize Counselman, so the treatment is based on the dissent's positive reference.

quote: What I have suggested as to the proper course of procedure in this court is supported by our action in Shoener v. Pennsylvania, 207 U. S. 188, 195.
rationale: Justice Harlan in his dissent cites Shoener v. Pennsylvania to support his argument about proper judicial procedure. The majority opinion does not directly cite or criticize Shoener, so the treatment is based on the dissent's positive reference.

quote: Our reaffirmation of Powell does not necessarily resolve the specific questions presented in these cases. For petitioners argue that whatever the constitutionality of additional qualifications for membership imposed by Congress, the historical and textual materials discussed in Powell do not support the conclusion that the Constitution prohibits additional qualifications imposed by States.
rationale: The Court reaffirms Powell's holding that Congress cannot add qualifications for its members beyond those in the Constitution, but acknowledges that Powell did not directly address whether States can add such qualifications, which is the central question in the current case.

targetName: U.S. Term Limits, Inc. v. Hill
quote: The judgment is affirmed. It is so ordered.
rationale: The Supreme Court explicitly affirms the judgment of the Arkansas Supreme Court, which had held that Amendment 73 violated the Federal Constitution.

quote: The provisions at issue in Storer and our other Elections Clause cases were thus constitutional because they regulated election procedures and did not even arguably impose any substantive qualification rendering a class of potential candidates ineligible for ballot position. They served the state interest in protecting the integrity and regularity of the election process, an interest independent of any attempt to evade the constitutional prohibition against the imposition of additional qualifications for service in Congress.
rationale: The Court distinguishes Storer by explaining that it involved procedural regulations rather than substantive qualifications, unlike the term limits at issue in the current case which attempt to add qualifications for congressional service.

quote: In McCulloch v. Maryland, 4 Wheat. 316 (1819), the Court rejected the argument that the Constitution's silence on the subject of state power to tax corporations chartered by Congress implies that the States have 'reserved' power to tax such federal instrumentalities. As Chief Justice Marshall pointed out, an 'original right to tax' such federal entities 'never existed, and the question whether it has been surrendered, cannot arise.'
rationale: The Court cites McCulloch to support its argument that states cannot claim to have reserved powers they never possessed before the Constitution, applying this principle to the question of whether states can add qualifications for federal representatives.

quote: More than a century ago, this Court was asked to invalidate a Michigan election law because it called for Presidential electors to be elected on a district-by-district basis rather than being chosen by 'the State' as a whole. See Art. II, § 1, cl. 2. Conceding that the Constitution might be ambiguous on this score, the Court asserted that 'where there is ambiguity or doubt, or where two views may well be entertained, contemporaneous and subsequent practical construction[s] are entitled to the greatest weight.'
rationale: The Court distinguishes McPherson by noting that while it gave weight to historical practice in that case, the historical evidence in the current case actually supports the conclusion that states cannot add qualifications for congressional representatives.

quote: In McCulloch, the Court rejected the argument that the Constitution's silence on the subject of state power to tax corporations chartered by Congress implies that the States have 'reserved' power to tax such federal instrumentalities. As Chief Justice Marshall pointed out, an 'original right to tax' such federal entities 'never existed, and the question whether it has been surrendered, cannot arise.' Id., at 430. See also Crandall v. Nevada, 6 Wall. 35, 46 (1868).
rationale: The Court cites Crandall as additional support for the principle that states cannot claim to have reserved powers they never possessed before the Constitution, applying this to the question of whether states can add qualifications for federal representatives.

targetName: State Ex Rel. Johnson v. Crane
quote: Our decision in Powell and its historical analysis were consistent with prior decisions from state courts. For example, in State ex rel. Johnson v. Crane, 65 Wyo. 189, 197 P. 2d 864 (1948), the Wyoming Supreme Court undertook a detailed historical analysis and concluded that the Qualifications Clauses were exclusive.
rationale: The Court cites Crane as a state court decision that reached the same conclusion about the exclusivity of the Qualifications Clauses, supporting the Court's position that states cannot add qualifications for federal representatives.

quote: This conclusion is consistent with our previous recognition that, in certain limited contexts, the power to regulate the incidents of the federal system is not a reserved power of the States, but rather is delegated by the Constitution. Thus, we have noted that '[w]hile, in a loose sense, the right to vote for representatives in Congress is sometimes spoken of as a right derived from the states, . . . this statement is true only in the sense that the states are authorized by the Constitution, to legislate on the subject as provided by § 2 of Art. I.'
rationale: The Court cites Classic to support its argument that the power to regulate federal elections is delegated by the Constitution rather than reserved by the states, which supports the conclusion that states cannot add qualifications for federal representatives.

targetName: Garcia v. San Antonio Metropolitan Transit Authority
quote: As we have frequently noted, '[t]he States unquestionably do retain a significant measure of sovereign authority. They do so, however, only to the extent that the Constitution has not divested them of their original powers and transferred those powers to the Federal Government.' Garcia v. San Antonio Metropolitan Transit Authority, 469 U. S. 528, 549 (1985) (internal quotation marks and citation omitted) (emphasis added).
rationale: The Court cites Garcia to support its argument that states retain sovereign authority only to the extent that the Constitution has not divested them of their original powers, applying this principle to the question of whether states can add qualifications for federal representatives.

targetName: Butchers' Benevolent Ass'n v. Crescent City Live-Stock Landing & Slaughter-House Co.
quote: In the Slaughter-House Cases, 16 Wall. 36, 78-80 (1873), the Court was careful to hold that federal citizenship in and of itself suffices for the assertion of rights under the Constitution, rights that stem from sources other than the States.
rationale: The Court cites the Slaughter-House Cases to support its argument that federal citizenship provides rights that stem from national rather than state sources, which supports the conclusion that states cannot add qualifications for federal representatives.

quote: Only two Terms ago we confirmed this understanding of Powell in Nixon v. United States, 506 U. S. 224 (1993). After noting that the three qualifications for membership specified in Art. I, § 2, are of 'a precise, limited nature' and 'unalterable by the legislature,' we explained: 'Our conclusion in Powell was based on the fixed meaning of '[qualifications' set forth in Art. I, § 2.'
rationale: The Court cites Nixon as confirming its interpretation of Powell that the qualifications for Congress are fixed in the Constitution and cannot be altered by the legislature, supporting the conclusion that states cannot add qualifications for federal representatives.

targetName: Byrd v. Blue Ridge Rural Electric Cooperative, Inc.
quote: In Byrd, the Court faced a one-or-the-other choice: trial by judge as in state court, or trial by jury according to the federal practice. In the case before us, a choice of that order is not required, for the principal state and federal interests can be accommodated.
rationale: The dissent cites Byrd as a precedent but does not criticize or negatively treat it. Justice Stevens acknowledges the case's relevance to the Seventh Amendment analysis while distinguishing the current case's circumstances.

targetName: Browning-Ferris Industries of Vermont, Inc. v. Kelco Disposal, Inc.
quote: We noted the Circuit decisions in point, id., at 157, n. 3, and, in Browning-Ferris, we again referred to appellate court abuse-of-discretion review
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Browning-Ferris as supporting precedent for the proposition that appellate courts can review district court excessiveness determinations using an abuse of discretion standard. The case is referenced positively without criticism.

targetName: Grunenthal v. Long Island Rail Road
quote: Dissenting from the Court's professed refusal to answer the question presented in Grunenthal v. Long Island R. Co., Justices Harlan and Stewart observed that in Grunenthal itself, this Court indeed had reviewed the refusal of the District Court to set aside a jury verdict for excessiveness.
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Grunenthal as a relevant precedent that addressed appellate review of jury verdicts. The dissent does not criticize the case but uses it to support the argument that appellate review of excessiveness is permissible.

quote: From the beginning, its language has been regarded as but subservient to the single purpose of the Amendment, to preserve the essentials of the jury trial in actions at law, serving to distinguish them from suits in equity and admiralty, see Parsons v. Bedford, 3 Pet. 433, 446
rationale: Justice Stevens quotes a prior opinion that cites Parsons to explain the purpose of the Seventh Amendment. The case is referenced positively as supporting authority without criticism.

quote: Although we stated in dicta that '[t]he proper role of the trial and appellate courts in the federal system in reviewing the size of jury verdicts is, however, a matter of federal law,' ibid., that broad statement was supported by citation to two cases, Hanna v. Plumer, 380 U. S. 460 (1965), and Byrd v. Blue Ridge Rural Elec. Cooperative, Inc., 356 U. S. 525 (1958), which did not involve the review of jury awards.
rationale: Justice Stevens mentions Hanna to point out that it was cited in Donovan but did not actually involve review of jury awards. The case is not criticized but is distinguished as not directly applicable to the issue at hand.

quote: In following that procedure here, the Court of Appeals did not reexamine any fact determined by a jury. 66 F. 3d, at 431. It merely identified that portion of the judgment that constitutes 'unlawful excess.' See Dimick v. Schiedt, 293 U. S. 474, 486 (1935).
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Dimick as supporting authority for the proposition that identifying an unlawful excess in a judgment does not constitute reexamining facts determined by a jury. The case is referenced positively without criticism.

targetName: Consorti v. Armstrong World Industries, Inc.
quote: The Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit correctly concluded in Consorti v. Armstrong World Industries, Inc., 64 F. 3d 781, superseded, 72 F. 3d 1003 (1995), that New York's excessiveness standard applies in federal court in diversity cases controlled by New York law.
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Consorti positively as correctly concluding that New York's excessiveness standard applies in federal diversity cases. The case is endorsed rather than criticized.

targetName: Savino Dagnello v. Long Island Rail Road Company
quote: If an appellate court may reverse a jury's damages award when its own conscience has been shocked, 66 F. 3d, at 430, or its sense of justice outraged, Dagnello v. Long Island R. Co., 289 F. 2d 797, 802 (CA2 1961)
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Dagnello as an example of a standard used by appellate courts to review jury awards. The case is referenced as a descriptive example without criticism.

quote: Consorti erred in basing that conclusion in part on the fact that a New York statute requires that State's appellate division to apply the standard, but it was nevertheless faithful to the Rules of Decision Act, as construed in Erie R. Co. v. Tompkins, 304 U. S. 64 (1938), in holding that a state-law limitation on the size of a judgment could not be ignored.
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Erie as the foundational case for the Rules of Decision Act, noting that Consorti was faithful to Erie's principles. The case is referenced positively as controlling authority.

quote: Our per curiam decision in Donovan v. Penn Shipping Co., 429 U. S. 648 (1977), provides no support for the proposition that federal appellate courts are confined to a federal standard of excessiveness.
rationale: Justice Stevens distinguishes Donovan, noting it doesn't support the proposition that federal appellate courts must use a federal excessiveness standard. The case is not criticized but is clarified as not applicable to the current issue.

quote: That contention is undermined by numerous cases in which the 'court above' granted new trials without making any reference to the trial judge's view of the damages. See, e. g., Honda Motor Co. v. Oberg, 512 U. S. 415, 422-425 (1994) (citing cases).
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Honda as providing examples of cases where courts granted new trials without deferring to trial judges' views. The case is referenced as supporting authority without criticism.

quote: Justice Scalia finds in Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 59 a 'federal standard' for new trial motions in 'direct collision' with, and 'leaving no room for the operation of,' a state law like CPLR § 5501(c). Post, at 468 (quoting Burlington Northern R. Co., 480 U. S., at 4-5).
rationale: Justice Stevens references Burlington Northern as being cited by Justice Scalia in his opinion. Stevens does not criticize the case itself but disagrees with Scalia's application of it to the current situation.

quote: Three times this Term we have assigned appellate courts the task of independently reviewing similarly mixed questions of law and fact. See Ornelas v. United States, 517 U. S. 690, 696-697 (1996)
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Ornelas as a recent example of the Court assigning appellate courts the task of independently reviewing mixed questions of law and fact. The case is referenced as supporting authority without criticism.

quote: We subsequently recognized that, even in cases in which the Erie doctrine was not in play — cases arising wholly under federal law— the question was not settled; we twice granted certiorari to decide the unsettled issue, but ultimately resolved the cases on other grounds. See Grunenthal v. Long Island R. Co., 393 U. S. 156, 158 (1968); Neese v. Southern R. Co., 350 U. S. 77 (1955).
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Neese as an example of a case where the Court granted certiorari on the issue of appellate review of jury verdicts but resolved the case on other grounds. The case is referenced as historical context without criticism.

quote: Federal courts have interpreted the Federal Rules, however, with sensitivity to important state interests and regulatory policies. See, e. g., Walker v. Armco Steel Corp., 446 U. S. 740, 750-752 (1980)
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Walker as an example of federal courts interpreting Federal Rules with sensitivity to state interests. The case is referenced positively as supporting authority.

quote: Early cases do state that the Reexamination Clause prohibits appellate review of excessive jury awards, but they do not foreclose the practice altogether. See, e. g., Southern Railway-Carolina Div. v. Bennett, 233 U. S. 80, 87 (1914)
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Bennett as an early case that discussed limitations on appellate review of jury awards but notes it did not completely foreclose such review. The case is referenced as historical context without criticism.

targetName: S.A. Healy Company v. Milwaukee Metropolitan Sewerage District
quote: In sum, § 5501(c) contains a procedural instruction, see supra, at 426, but the State's objective is manifestly substantive. Cf. S. A. Healy Co. v. Milwaukee Metropolitan Sewerage Dist., 60 F. 3d 305, 310 (CA7 1995).
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Healy as a comparative reference for the proposition that a state law can have a substantive objective despite procedural elements. The case is referenced without criticism.

quote: Indeed, in Ismail v. Cohen, 899 F. 2d 183 (1990), the authority upon which Justice Scalia relies, the Second Circuit stated that district courts test damage awards for excessiveness under the 'shock the conscience' standard.
rationale: Justice Stevens mentions Ismail as a case relied upon by Justice Scalia that discusses the 'shock the conscience' standard. The case itself is not criticized, though Stevens disagrees with Scalia's use of it.

quote: As a matter of federal-court administration, we have recognized in other contexts the need for according some deference to the lower court's resolution of legal, yet fact-intensive, questions. See Ornelas v. United States, 517 U. S., at 699; Pierce v. Underwood, 487 U. S. 552, 558, n. 1 (1988).
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Pierce as an example of the Court recognizing the need for deference to lower courts on fact-intensive legal questions. The case is referenced positively as supporting authority.

targetName: BMW of North America, Inc. v. Gore
quote: For rights that are state created, state law governs the amount properly awarded as punitive damages, subject to an ultimate federal constitutional check for exorbitancy. See BMW of North America, Inc. v. Gore, 517 U. S. 559, 568 (1996)
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Gore as establishing that state law governs punitive damages awards subject to constitutional limits. The case is referenced as controlling authority without criticism.

targetName: MARKMAN Et Al. v. WESTVIEW INSTRUMENTS, INC., Et Al.
quote: Three times this Term we have assigned appellate courts the task of independently reviewing similarly mixed questions of law and fact. See Ornelas v. United States, 517 U. S. 690, 696-697 (1996); Markman v. Westview Instruments, Inc., 517 U. S. 370, 388-390 (1996)
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Markman as a recent example of the Court assigning appellate courts the task of independently reviewing mixed questions of law and fact. The case is referenced as supporting authority without criticism.

quote: Guaranty Trust Co. v. York, 326 U. S. 99 (1945), an early interpretation of Erie, propounded an 'outcome-determination' test: '[D]oes it significantly affect the result of a litigation for a federal court to disregard a law of a State that would be controlling in an action upon the same claim by the same parties in a State court?'
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Guaranty Trust as an early interpretation of Erie that established the 'outcome-determination' test. The case is referenced as important precedent without criticism.

quote: Such appellate review is proper because mixed questions require courts to construe all record inferences in favor of the fact-finder's decision and then to determine whether, on the facts as found below, the legal standard has been met. See Orelas, 517 U. S., at 696-697 (quoting Pullman-Standard v. Swint, 456 U. S. 273, 289, n. 19 (1982)).
rationale: Justice Stevens notes that Ornelas quoted Pullman-Standard regarding how courts should review mixed questions of law and fact. The case is referenced as supporting authority without criticism.

quote: Ordering application of a state statute of limitations to an equity proceeding in federal court, the Court said in Guaranty Trust: '[W]here a federal court is exercising jurisdiction solely because of the diversity of citizenship of the parties, the outcome of the litigation in the federal court should be substantially the same, so far as legal rules determine the outcome of a litigation, as it would be if tried in a State court.'
rationale: This is a duplicate entry for Guaranty Trust Co. v. York (already covered in uniqueID 1116658). The treatment is the same - cited positively as important precedent.

quote: Because there is no conceivable conflict between Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 59 and the application of the New York damages limit, this ease is controlled by Erie and the Rules of Decision Act, rather than by the Rules Enabling Act's limitation on federal procedural rules that conflict with state substantive rights. See Ely, The Irrepressible Myth of Erie, 87 Harv. L. Rev. 693, 698 (1974); see also Sibbach v. Wilson & Co., 312 U. S. 1 (1941).
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Sibbach in relation to the Rules Enabling Act's limitations. The case is referenced as relevant authority without criticism.

quote: If the meaning of the Seventh Amendment were fixed at 1791, our civil juries would remain, as they unquestionably were at common law, 'twelve good men and true,' 3 W. Blackstone, Commentaries *349; see Capital Traction Co. v. Hof, 174 U. S. 1, 13 (1899)
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Hof as supporting the historical understanding of jury composition. The case is referenced as historical context without criticism.

targetName: ætna Casualty & Surety Co. v. Yeatts
quote: see also Aetna Casualty & Surety Co. v. Yeatts, 122 F. 2d 350, 353 (CA4 1941) ('The exercise of [the trial court's power to set aside the jury's verdict and grant a new trial] is not in derogation of the right of trial by jury but is one of the historic safeguards of that right.')
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Yeatts for the proposition that a trial court's power to set aside jury verdicts is a safeguard of the jury trial right. The case is referenced positively as supporting authority.

quote: see also Blunt v. Little, 3 F. Cas. 760, 761-762 (No. 1,578) (CC Mass. 1822) (Story, J.) ('[I]f it should clearly appear that the jury have committed a gross error, or have acted from improper motives, or have given damages excessive in relation to the person or the injury, it is as much the duty of the court to interfere, to prevent the wrong, as in any other case.')
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Blunt as historical precedent establishing a court's duty to interfere when a jury has given excessive damages. The case is referenced positively as supporting authority.

targetName: Ragan v. Merchants Transfer & Warehouse Co.
quote: Just as the Erie principle precludes a federal court from giving a state-created claim 'longer life . . . than [the claim] would have had in the state court,' Ragan, 337 U. S., at 533-534, so Erie precludes a recovery in federal court significantly larger than the recovery that would have been tolerated in state court.
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Ragan as establishing that Erie prevents federal courts from extending the life of state claims. The case is referenced positively as supporting authority for applying the same principle to damage awards.

quote: But see Colgrove v. Battin, 413 U. S. 149, 160 (1973) (six-member jury for civil trials satisfies Seventh Amendment's guarantee).
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Colgrove as an example of the Court accepting procedures not in conformity with common law when the Seventh Amendment was adopted. The case is referenced without criticism as an example of constitutional evolution.

quote: The Seventh Amendment, which governs proceedings in federal court, but not in state court, bears not only on the allocation of trial functions between judge and jury, the issue in Byrd; it also controls the allocation of authority to review verdicts, the issue of concern here. The Amendment reads: 'In Suits at common law, where the value in controversy shall exceed twenty dollars, the right of trial by jury shall be preserved, and no fact tried by a jury, shall be otherwise re-examined in any Court of the United States, than according to the rules of the common law.' U. S. Const., Arndt. 7. Byrd involved the first Clause of the Amendment, the 'trial by jury' Clause. This case involves the second, the 're-examination' Clause. In keeping with the historic understanding, the Reexamination Clause does not inhibit the authority of trial judges to grant new trials 'for any of the reasons for which new trials have heretofore been granted in actions at law in the courts of the United States.' Fed. Rule Civ. Proc. 59(a).
rationale: Justice Stevens mentions Walker in a footnote (footnote 14) as establishing that the Seventh Amendment governs federal but not state court proceedings. The case is referenced as established precedent without criticism.

targetName: Alonzo Wayne Taylor v. The Washington Terminal Company
quote: Trial judges have the 'unique opportunity to consider the evidence in the living courtroom context,' Taylor v. Washington Terminal Co., 409 F. 2d 145, 148 (CADC 1969), while appellate judges see only the 'cold paper record,' 66 F. 3d, at 431.
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Taylor for the proposition that trial judges have a unique perspective on evidence. The case is referenced positively as supporting authority for giving deference to trial judges.

targetName: Santo Scala v. Moore McCormack Lines, Inc.
quote: see also Scala v. Moore McCormack Lines, Inc., 985 F. 2d 680, 683 (CA2 1993) ('[I]n the federal courts, a judgment cannot stand where the damages awarded are so excessive as to shock the judicial conscience.')
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Scala as an example of the Second Circuit's standard for reviewing excessive damages. The case is referenced descriptively without criticism.

targetName: Theresa Davis v. Dr. Akin Omitowoju, Theresa Davis v. Dr. Akin Omitowoju
quote: While we have not specifically addressed the issue, courts of appeals have held that district court application of state statutory caps in diversity cases, postverdict, does not violate the Seventh Amendment. See Davis v. Omitowoju, 883 F. 2d 1155, 1161-1165 (CA3 1989) (Reexamination Clause of Seventh Amendment does not impede federal court's postverdict application of statutory cap)
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Davis as an example of a circuit court holding that applying state statutory caps does not violate the Seventh Amendment. The case is referenced as supporting authority without criticism.

quote: While we have not specifically addressed the issue, courts of appeals have held that district court application of state statutory caps in diversity cases, postverdict, does not violate the Seventh Amendment. See Davis v. Omitowoju, 883 F. 2d 1155, 1161-1165 (CA3 1989) (Reexamination Clause of Seventh Amendment does not impede federal court's postverdict application of statutory cap); Boyd v. Bulala, 877 F. 2d 1191, 1196 (CA4 1989) (postverdict application of statutory cap does not violate Seventh Amendment right of trial by jury).
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Boyd as another example of a circuit court holding that applying state statutory caps does not violate the Seventh Amendment. The case is referenced as supporting authority without criticism.

targetName: Will Holmes v. Elgin, Joliet & Eastern Railway Company
quote: All other Circuits agree. See, e. g., Holmes v. Elgin, Joliet & Eastern R. Co., 18 F. 3d 1393, 1396 (CA7 1994)
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Holmes as an example of a circuit court agreeing that appellate courts can review district court excessiveness determinations. The case is referenced as supporting authority without criticism.

quote: see also Lightfoot v. Union Carbide Corp., 901 F. Supp. 166, 169 (SDNY 1995) (CPLR 5501(c)'s 'materially deviates' standard 'is pretty well established as applicable to [state] trial and appellate courts.')
rationale: Justice Stevens cites Lightfoot as establishing that New York's 'materially deviates' standard applies to both trial and appellate courts. The case is referenced as supporting authority without criticism.

targetName: William Gasperini v. The Center for Humanities, Inc., Doing Business as Guidance Associates
targetTreatment: Affirmed in part; Reversed in part by
quote: While I agree with most of the reasoning in the Court's opinion, I disagree with its disposition of the case. I would affirm the judgment of the Court of Appeals.
rationale: Justice Stevens states he would affirm the Court of Appeals judgment rather than vacate and remand as the majority does. This indicates he agrees with part of the majority's reasoning but disagrees with its ultimate disposition, constituting a partial affirmance and partial reversal.

quote: In federal courts of equity the doctrine of laches was early supplemented by the rule that when the question is of lapse of time barring relief in equity, such courts... will nevertheless, when consonant with equitable principles, adopt and apply as their own, the local statute of limitations applicable to the equitable causes of action
rationale: The court cites McDonald as an example of applying state statutes of limitations to equity suits brought in aid of legal rights, but does not criticize or limit the case.

quote: see Southern Pacific Co. v. Boegert, 250 U.S. 483, 39 S.Ct. 533, 63 L.Ed. 1099, where no statute of limitations was pleaded; Id., 2 Cir., 244 F. 61, 65.
rationale: The court cites Southern Pacific as an example where the doctrine of laches was applied in the absence of a statute of limitations, without any negative treatment.

targetName: Hanover Fire Insurance v. Morse Dry Dock & Repair Co.
quote: In Hanover Fire Insurance Co. v. Morse Dry Dock & Repair Co., 270 N.Y. 86, 200 N.E. 589, the Court of Appeals declared... 'The exception is not applicable in cases of concurrent jurisdiction, however, if a party's remedy at law is inadequate and imperfect and he is required to go into equity to procure complete and adequate relief.'
rationale: The court cites Hanover Fire Insurance as persuasive authority on when the ten-year statute of limitations applies in equity cases under New York law, without any negative treatment.

quote: This Court has recognized that this statute is a bar to actions at law and has so applied it in suits to recover assessments on shareholders of a bank. See Platt v. Wilmot, supra.
rationale: The court cites Platt as recognizing that the three-year statute is a bar to actions at law, without criticizing or limiting the case.

quote: From the beginning, equity, in the absence of any statute of limitations made applicable to equity suits, has provided its own rule of limitations through the doctrine of laches, the principle that equity will not aid a plaintiff whose unexcused delay, if the suit were allowed, would be prejudicial to the defendant. Wagner v. Baird, 7 How. 234, 258, 12 L.Ed. 681
rationale: The court cites Wagner as supporting the principle that equity provides its own rule of limitations through the doctrine of laches, without any negative treatment.

quote: In federal courts of equity the doctrine of laches was early supplemented by the rule that when the question is of lapse of time barring relief in equity, such courts... will nevertheless, when consonant with equitable principles, adopt and apply as their own, the local statute of limitations applicable to the equitable causes of action in the judicial district in which the case is heard. Bacon v. Howard, 20 How. 22, 26, 15 L.Ed. 811; Clarke v. Boormans Executors, 18 Wall. 493, 505, 506, 21 L.Ed. 904
rationale: The court cites Clarke as supporting the principle that federal courts of equity may adopt local statutes of limitations, without any negative treatment.

quote: Even though there is no state statute applicable to similar equitable demands, when the jurisdiction of the federal court is concurrent with that of law, or the suit is brought in aid of a legal right, equity will withhold its remedy if the legal right is barred by the local statute of limitations... Michoud v. Girod, 4 How, 503, 561, 11 L.Ed. 1076
rationale: The court cites Michoud as supporting the principle that equity will withhold its remedy when a legal right is barred by a local statute of limitations, without any negative treatment.

quote: In Potter v. Walker, 276 N.Y. 15, 11 N.E.2d 335, the court said... 'In respect to those causes of action by which is sought to recover profits received by directors by reason of wrongful acts, an action at law would not afford adequate relief. To the extent that an accounting is necessary, the right and the remedy must necessarily be of an equitable nature.'
rationale: The court cites Potter as persuasive authority on when the ten-year statute of limitations applies in equity cases under New York law, without any negative treatment.

targetName: Kirby v. Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Railroad
quote: But where the equity jurisdiction is exclusive and is not exercised in aid or support of a legal right, state statutes of limitations barring actions at law are inapplicable, and in the absence of any state statute barring the equitable remedy in like cases, the federal court is remitted to and applies the doctrine of laches as controlling... Kirby v. Lake Shore & Michigan Southern R. Co., 120 U.S. 130, 139, 7 S.Ct. 430, 435, 30 L.Ed. 569
