Fowler v. Rhode Island, 345 U. S. 67; Niemotko v. Maryland, 340 U. S. 268.
rationale: The dissent cites Niemotko to establish that barring religious groups from public property violates constitutional guarantees. The citation is used supportively to establish a constitutional principle without criticism.

targetName: Two Guys From Harrison-Allentown, Inc. v. McGinley
quote: We are under a duty to interpret these provisions so as to render them constitutional if reasonably possible. Compare Two Guys v. McGinley, 366 U. S. 582, 592-595; Everson v. Board of Education, 330 U. S. 1, 4, and n. 2.
rationale: The dissent cites Two Guys to establish the principle that courts should interpret laws to preserve their constitutionality when possible. The citation is used supportively to establish a judicial principle without criticism.

quote: These are not, it must be stressed, cases like Brown v. Board of Education, 347 U. S. 483, in which this Court held that, in the sphere of public education, the Fourteenth Amendment's guarantee of equal protection of the laws required that race not be treated as a relevant factor.
rationale: The dissent explicitly distinguishes the current case from Brown, noting that while racial segregation is inherently unequal, religious accommodation is constitutionally required. This creates a clear distinction between the precedents.

quote: We have long held that 'an act denounced as a crime by both national and state sovereignties is an offense against the peace and dignity of both and may be punished by each.' United States v. Lanza, 260 U. S. 377, 382 (1922). Decades later, a sharply divided Court reaffirmed this separate-sovereigns doctrine. Abbate v. United States, 359 U. S. 187 (1959); Bartkus v. Illinois, 359 U. S. 121 (1959).
rationale: The Court cites Bartkus as precedent that reaffirmed the separate-sovereigns doctrine, without criticizing or questioning its validity. The Court ultimately upholds this doctrine in the present case.

quote: We have long held that 'an act denounced as a crime by both national and state sovereignties is an offense against the peace and dignity of both and may be punished by each.' United States v. Lanza, 260 U. S. 377, 382 (1922).
rationale: The Court directly quotes and relies on Lanza as establishing the separate-sovereigns doctrine, which it upholds in the present case.

quote: Recalling that the Fifth Amendment prohibits double jeopardy not 'for the same ac[t]' but 'for the same offence,' and that '[a]n offence, in its legal signification, means the transgression of a law,' id., at 19, we drew the now-familiar inference: A single act 'may be an offence or transgression of the laws of' two sovereigns, and hence punishable by both.
rationale: The Court cites Moore favorably as establishing the principle that a single act can constitute separate offenses under different sovereigns' laws, which supports the dual-sovereignty doctrine upheld in this case.

quote: But as we later explained, 'that language by Mr. Justice Washington reflected his belief that the state statute imposed state sanctions for violation of a federal criminal law. As he viewed the matter, the two trials would not be of similar crimes arising out of the same conduct; they would be of the same crime.'
rationale: The Court distinguishes Houston by explaining that it involved a unique situation where a state was prosecuting a federal offense, not a case where state and federal governments were prosecuting separate offenses based on the same conduct.

quote: Eliminating the dual-sovereignty rule would do little to trim the reach of federal criminal law, and it would not even prevent many successive state and federal prosecutions for the same criminal conduct unless we also overruled the long-settled rule that an 'offence' for double jeopardy purposes is defined by statutory elements, not by what might be described in a looser sense as a unit of criminal conduct. See Blockburger v. United States, 284 U. S. 299 (1932).
rationale: The Court cites Blockburger as establishing the test for determining whether two offenses are the same for double jeopardy purposes, without questioning its validity.

quote: We cemented that foundation 70 years after the last of those antebellum cases, in a decision upholding a federal prosecution that followed one by a State. See United States v. Lanza, 260 U. S. 377, 382 (1922). And for decades more, we applied our precedent without qualm or quibble. See, e.g., Screws v. United States, 325 U. S. 91 (1945); Jerome v. United States, 318 U. S. 101 (1943); Puerto Rico v. Shell Co. (P. R.), Ltd., 302 U. S. 253 (1937); Westfall v. United States, 274 U. S. 256 (1927); Hebert v. Louisiana, 272 U. S. 312 (1926). When petitioners in 1959 asked us twice to reverse course, we twice refused, finding '[n]o consideration or persuasive reason not presented to the Court in the prior cases' for disturbing our 'firmly established' doctrine. Abbate v. United States, 359 U. S. 187, 195.
rationale: The Court cites Abbate as precedent that reaffirmed the separate-sovereigns doctrine, which it upholds in the present case.

quote: Between 1847 and 1850, the Court decided a pair of cases, United States v. Marigold and Fox v. Ohio. While addressing other matters in those decisions, the Court offered passing approval to the possibility of successive state and federal prosecutions, but did so without analysis and without actually upholding a successive conviction.
rationale: The Court acknowledges Fox as an early case that suggested the possibility of successive state and federal prosecutions, though it notes the case did not directly uphold such a prosecution.

quote: Incorporation of the Clause as a restraint on action by the States, effected in Benton v. Maryland, 395 U. S. 784 (1969), has rendered this rationale obsolete.
rationale: The Court cites Benton as establishing that the Double Jeopardy Clause applies to the states, but does not question its validity. Rather, it explains why incorporation does not undermine the separate-sovereigns doctrine.

quote: There is a difference between the whole and a single part, and that difference underlies decisions as foundational to our legal system as McCulloch v. Maryland, 4 Wheat. 316 (1819). There, in terms so directly relevant as to seem presciently tailored to answer this very objection, Chief Justice Marshall distinguished precisely between 'the people of a State' and '[t]he people of all the States,' id., at 428, 435.
rationale: The Court cites McCulloch favorably to support its view of federalism and the distinction between state and federal sovereignty, which underpins the separate-sovereigns doctrine.

quote: That 'Power' is—as Chief Justice Marshall put it—the power 'to say what the law is' in the context of a particular 'case' or 'controversy' before the court. Marbury v. Madison, 1 Cranch 137, 177 (1803); Art. III, §2.
rationale: Justice Thomas cites Marbury in his concurrence to describe the nature of judicial power, but this does not represent the Court's treatment of the case.

quote: Once the Fourth Amendment was held to apply to the States as well as the Federal Government, however, the silver-platter doctrine was scuttled. See Elkins v. United States, 364 U. S. 206 (1960); Wolf v. Colorado, 338 U. S. 25 (1949). Now the fruits of unreasonable state searches are inadmissible in federal and state courts alike.
rationale: Justice Ginsburg in her dissent distinguishes Elkins, noting that while the Court abandoned the silver-platter doctrine after Fourth Amendment incorporation, it has not similarly abandoned the separate-sovereigns doctrine after Double Jeopardy Clause incorporation.

quote: The separate-sovereigns doctrine, I acknowledge, has been embraced repeatedly by the Court. But '[s]tare decisis is not an inexorable command.' Payne v. Tennessee, 501 U. S. 808, 828 (1991).
rationale: Justice Ginsburg cites Payne in her dissent to argue that stare decisis should not prevent overruling the separate-sovereigns doctrine, but this does not represent the Court's treatment of the case.

quote: Perhaps the most egregious example of this illegitimate use of stare decisis can be found in our 'substantive due process' jurisprudence. McDonald v. Chicago, 561 U. S. 742, 811 (2010) (THOMAS, J., concurring in part and concurring in judgment).
rationale: Justice Thomas cites McDonald in his concurrence to criticize substantive due process jurisprudence, but this does not represent the Court's treatment of the case.

quote: '[T]he language of the Clause . . . protects individuals from being twice put in jeopardy 'for the same offence,' not for the same conduct or actions,' Grady v. Corbin, 495 U. S. 508, 529 (1990), as Justice Scalia wrote in a soon-vindicated dissent, see United States v. Dixon, 509 U. S. 688 (1993) (overruling Grady).
rationale: The Court cites Justice Scalia's dissent in Grady, noting that it was later vindicated when Grady was overruled by Dixon. This supports the Court's textual analysis of the Double Jeopardy Clause.

quote: But because this Court has long held that two offenses 'are not the 'same offence' ' for double jeopardy purposes if 'prosecuted by different sovereigns,' Heath v. Alabama, 474 U. S. 82, 92 (1985), the District Court denied Gamble's motion to dismiss.
rationale: The Court cites Heath as establishing that offenses prosecuted by different sovereigns are not the 'same offence' for double jeopardy purposes, which is the principle it upholds in this case.

quote: Piracy was understood as a violation of the law of nations, which was seen as common to all. That is why any successive prosecution for piracy, being under the same law, would have been for the same offense. See United States v. Smith, 5 Wheat. 153, 163, n. a (1820) (quoting definitions of piracy by several ancient and more recent authorities).
rationale: The Court cites Smith in a footnote to explain why piracy was considered an offense against universal law, distinguishing it from ordinary crimes that can be separate offenses under different sovereigns' laws.

quote: In the face of so much contrary authority, the Court winds up leaning heavily on a single 1794 North Carolina Superior Court decision, State v. Brown. But the Court's choice here is revealing. True, Brown said that a verdict in North Carolina would not be 'pleadable in bar to an indictment preferred against [the defendant] in the Territory South of the Ohio.' But the Court leaves out what happened next. Brown went on to reject concurrent jurisdiction because trying the defendant 'according to the several laws of each State' could result in him being 'cropped in one, branded and whipped in another, imprisoned in a third, and hanged in a fourth; and all for one and the same offence.' The North Carolina court viewed that result as 'against natural justice' and 'therefore [could] not believe it to be law.'
rationale: Justice Gorsuch in his dissent argues that Brown actually supports his position against the separate-sovereigns doctrine, distinguishing the Court's interpretation of this case.

quote: We have long enforced this right by barring courts from relying on evidence gathered in an illegal search. Thus, in Weeks v. United States, 232 U. S. 383, 391–393 (1914), the Court held that federal prosecutors could not rely on the fruits of an unreasonable search undertaken by federal agents.
rationale: Justice Ginsburg in her dissent cites Weeks as establishing the exclusionary rule for federal courts, drawing an analogy to the evolution of Fourth Amendment doctrine, but this does not represent the Court's treatment of the case.

targetName: Osborn v. Bank of United States
quote: 'Judicial power is never exercised for the purpose of giving effect to the will of the Judge; always for the purpose of giving effect to the will of the Legislature; or, in other words, to the will of the law.' Osborn v. Bank of United States, 9 Wheat. 738, 866 (1824) (Marshall, C. J.).
rationale: Justice Thomas cites Osborn in his concurrence to describe the proper role of judicial power, but this does not represent the Court's treatment of the case.

quote: Stare decisis has many virtues, but when it comes to enforcing the Constitution this Court must take (and always has taken) special care in the doctrine's application. After all, judges swear to protect and defend the Constitution, not to protect what it prohibits. And while we rightly pay heed to the considered views of those who have come before us, especially in close cases, stare decisis isn't supposed to be 'the art of being methodically ignorant of what everyone knows.' Indeed, blind obedience to stare decisis would leave this Court still abiding grotesque errors like Dred Scott v. Sandford, Plessy v. Ferguson, and Korematsu v. United States.
rationale: Justice Gorsuch in his dissent criticizes Dred Scott as a 'grotesque error' that should not be followed under stare decisis principles, but this does not represent the Court's treatment of the case.

quote: Between 1847 and 1850, the Court decided a pair of cases, United States v. Marigold and Fox v. Ohio. While addressing other matters in those decisions, the Court offered passing approval to the possibility of successive state and federal prosecutions, but did so without analysis and without actually upholding a successive conviction.
rationale: The Court acknowledges Marigold as an early case that suggested the possibility of successive state and federal prosecutions, though it notes the case did not directly uphold such a prosecution.

quote: In United States v. Furlong, 5 Wheat. 184, 197 (1820), we said that an acquittal of piracy in the court of any 'civilized State' would bar prosecution in any other nation because piracy, as an 'offence within the criminal jurisdiction of all nations,' is 'punished by all.'
rationale: The Court cites Furlong to explain that piracy was considered an offense against universal law, but distinguishes it from ordinary crimes that can be separate offenses under different sovereigns' laws.

targetName: United States v. All Assets of G.P.S. Automotive Corp.
quote: That is a peculiar way to look at the Double Jeopardy Clause, which by its terms safeguards the 'person' and restrains the government. See, e.g., id., at 155; United States v. All Assets of G.P.S. Automotive Corp., 66 F. 3d 483, 498 (CA2 1995) (Calabresi, J., concurring).
rationale: Justice Ginsburg in her dissent cites this case to support her view that the Double Jeopardy Clause protects individuals rather than governments, but this does not represent the Court's treatment of the case.

quote: Our adherence to precedent is weakest in cases 'concerning procedural rules that implicate fundamental constitutional protections.' Alleyne v. United States, 570 U. S. 99, 116, n. 5 (2013).
rationale: Justice Ginsburg in her dissent cites Alleyne to argue that stare decisis has less force in cases involving constitutional protections, but this does not represent the Court's treatment of the case.

quote: And this Court has long rejected the idea that 'law enforcement reliance interests outweigh[h] the interest in protecting individual constitutional rights so as to warrant fidelity to an unjustifiable rule.' Instead, '[i]f it is clear that a practice is unlawful, individuals' interest in its discontinuance clearly outweighs any law enforcement 'entitlement' to its persistence.'
rationale: Justice Gorsuch in his dissent cites Gant to argue that law enforcement reliance interests should not outweigh constitutional rights, but this does not represent the Court's treatment of the case.

quote: What is more, the 'underpinnings' of the separate sovereigns exception have been 'erode[d] by subsequent decisions of this Court.' When this Court decided Moore, Lanza, Bartkus, and Abbate, the Double Jeopardy Clause applied only to the federal government under this Court's decision in Palko v. Connecticut.
rationale: Justice Ginsburg in her dissent cites Gaudin to argue that the foundations of the separate-sovereigns doctrine have been eroded, but this does not represent the Court's treatment of the case.

quote: As we explained last Term: 'When the original States declared their independence, they claimed the powers inherent in sovereignty . . . . The Constitution limited but did not abolish the sovereign powers of the States, which retained 'a residuary and inviolable sovereignty.' The Federalist No. 39, p. 245 (C. Rossiter ed. 1961). Thus, both the Federal Government and the States wield sovereign powers, and that is why our system of government is said to be one of 'dual sovereignty.' Gregory v. Ashcroft, 501 U. S. 452, 457 (1991).' Murphy v. National Collegiate Athletic Assn., 584 U. S. ___ , ___ (2018) (slip op., at 14).
rationale: The Court cites Alden (through a quote from Murphy) to support its view of federalism and the dual sovereignty structure of the American system, which underpins the separate-sovereigns doctrine.

targetName: Murphy v. Waterfront Commission of New York Harbor
quote: After application of the self-incrimination privilege to the States, the Court concluded that its prior position was incompatible with the 'policies and purposes' of the privilege. Murphy v. Waterfront Comm'n of N. Y. Harbor, 378 U. S. 52, 55, 77 (1964). No longer, the Court held, could a witness 'be whipsawed into incriminating himself under both state and federal law even though the constitutional privilege against self-incrimination is applicable to each.' Id., at 55 (internal quotation marks omitted; emphasis added).
rationale: Justice Ginsburg in her dissent distinguishes Murphy, noting that while the Court abandoned its prior self-incrimination doctrine after Fifth Amendment incorporation, it has not similarly abandoned the separate-sovereigns doctrine after Double Jeopardy Clause incorporation.

quote: The inquiry attempts to quantify the unquantifiable and, by frequently sweeping in subjective factors, provides a ready means of justifying whatever result five Members of the Court seek to achieve. See Holder v. Hall, 512 U. S. 874, 943–944 (1994) (THOMAS, J., concurring in judgment) (describing a 'totality of circumstances' test as 'an empty incantation—a mere conjurer's trick'); Lawrence v. Texas, 539 U. S. 558, 577 (2003) (acknowledging that stare decisis is 'a principle of policy and not a mechanical formula').
rationale: Justice Thomas cites Lawrence in his concurrence to criticize the Court's multifactor stare decisis approach, but this does not represent the Court's treatment of the case.

quote: As the Court suggests, Congress is responsible for the proliferation of duplicative prosecutions for the same offenses by the States and the Federal Government. Ante, at 28. By legislating beyond its limited powers, Congress has taken from the People authority that they never gave. U. S. Const., Art. I, §8; The Federalist No. 22, p. 152 (C. Rossiter ed. 1961) ('all legitimate authority' derives from 'the consent of the people' (capitalization omitted)). And the Court has been complicit by blessing this questionable expansion of the Commerce Clause. See, e.g., Gonzales v. Raich, 545 U. S. 1, 57–74 (2005) (THOMAS, J., dissenting).
rationale: Justice Thomas in his concurrence criticizes the Court's Commerce Clause jurisprudence, including Raich, for enabling federal overreach, but this does not represent the Court's treatment of the case.

quote: And the strength of the case for adhering to such decisions grows in proportion to their 'antiquity.' Montejo v. Louisiana, 556 U. S. 778, 792 (2009).
rationale: The Court cites Montejo to support its stare decisis analysis, noting that the strength of precedent grows with its age.

quote: But even in constitutional cases, a departure from precedent 'demands special justification.' Arizona v. Rumsey, 467 U. S. 203, 212 (1984).
rationale: The Court cites Rumsey to support its stare decisis analysis, noting that overruling precedent requires special justification.

quote: This principle resonates throughout our history and law. State courts that refused to entertain federal causes of action found little sympathy when attempting the very separate sovereigns theory underlying today's decision.
rationale: Justice Gorsuch in his dissent cites Testa to argue against the separate-sovereigns doctrine, but this does not represent the Court's treatment of the case.

quote: The inquiry attempts to quantify the unquantifiable and, by frequently sweeping in subjective factors, provides a ready means of justifying whatever result five Members of the Court seek to achieve. See Holder v. Hall, 512 U. S. 874, 943–944 (1994) (THOMAS, J., concurring in judgment) (describing a 'totality of circumstances' test as 'an empty incantation—a mere conjurer's trick').
rationale: Justice Thomas cites his own concurrence in Holder in his concurrence here to criticize the Court's multifactor stare decisis approach, but this does not represent the Court's treatment of the case.

quote: '[T]he language of the Clause . . . protects individuals from being twice put in jeopardy 'for the same offence,' not for the same conduct or actions,' Grady v. Corbin, 495 U. S. 508, 529 (1990), as Justice Scalia wrote in a soon-vindicated dissent, see United States v. Dixon, 509 U. S. 688 (1993) (overruling Grady).
rationale: The Court cites Dixon as having overruled Grady, which supports its textual analysis of the Double Jeopardy Clause focusing on 'offence' rather than conduct.

targetName: New Energy Co. of Indiana v. Limbach
quote: The Commerce Clause does not prohibit all state action designed to give its residents an advantage in the marketplace, but only action of that description in connection with the State's regulation of interstate commerce. Direct subsidization of domestic industry does not ordinarily run afoul of that prohibition; discriminatory taxation . . . does.
rationale: The Court cites New Energy Co. to distinguish between permissible subsidies and impermissible discriminatory taxation, using it as supporting precedent for its analysis rather than criticizing or limiting it.

targetName: West Lynn Creamery, Inc. v. Healy
quote: We have 'never squarely confronted the constitutionality of subsidies,' id., at 199, n. 15, and we need not address these questions today. Assuming, arguendo, that the Town is correct that a direct subsidy benefiting only those nonprofits serving principally Maine residents would be permissible, our cases do not sanction a tax exemption serving similar ends.
rationale: The Court cites West Lynn Creamery to acknowledge the open question about subsidies while using its reasoning to distinguish between subsidies and tax exemptions. The citation supports rather than criticizes the target case.

targetName: City of Philadelphia v. New Jersey
quote: In Philadelphia v. New Jersey, 437 U. S. 617 (1978), we struck down a New Jersey statute prohibiting certain categories of out-of-state waste from flowing into the State's landfills, noting that 'a State may not accord its own inhabitants a preferred right of access over consumers in other States to natural resources located within its borders.'
rationale: The Court cites Philadelphia v. New Jersey as supporting precedent for the principle that states cannot discriminate against out-of-state consumers in access to in-state resources. The citation reinforces rather than criticizes the target case.

quote: As we made clear most recently in Fulton Corp. v. Faulkner, 516 U. S., at 333, n. 3, there is no 'de minimis' defense to a charge of discriminatory taxation under the Commerce Clause.
rationale: The Court cites Fulton Corp. as authoritative precedent for the principle that there is no 'de minimis' defense to discriminatory taxation under the Commerce Clause. The citation reinforces rather than criticizes the target case.

quote: Avoiding this sort of 'economic Balkanization,' Hughes v. Oklahoma, 441 U. S., at 325, and the retaliatory acts of other States that may follow, is one of the central purposes of our negative Commerce Clause jurisprudence.
rationale: The Court cites Hughes v. Oklahoma to support its explanation of the purpose of the dormant Commerce Clause. The citation reinforces rather than criticizes the target case.

targetName: Camps Newfound/Owatonna, Inc. v. Town of Harrison
quote: The judgment of the Maine Supreme Judicial Court is reversed.
rationale: The Supreme Court explicitly reverses the Maine Supreme Judicial Court's decision, which had upheld the tax exemption statute that discriminated against camps serving primarily out-of-state residents.

quote: Contrary to Justice Scalia's suggestion, this case is quite unlike General Motors Corp. v. Tracy, 519 U. S. 278 (1997). There, the Court premised its holding that the statute at issue was not facially discriminatory on the view that sellers of 'bundled' and 'unbundled' natural gas were principally competing in different markets.
rationale: The Court explicitly distinguishes Tracy from the present case by noting that Tracy involved entities operating in different markets, whereas the Maine statute discriminates between identically situated camps based solely on whether they serve in-state or out-of-state campers.

quote: In Alexandria Scrap we concluded that the State of Maryland had, in effect, entered the market for abandoned automobile hulks as a purchaser because it was using state funds to provide bounties for their removal from Maryland streets and junkyards. Id., at 809-810. [...] Maine's tax exemption statute cannot be characterized as a proprietary activity falling within the market-participant exception.
rationale: The Court distinguishes Alexandria Scrap by explaining that while Maryland was acting as a market participant in that case, Maine's tax exemption cannot be characterized as proprietary activity and thus does not fall within the market-participant exception established in Alexandria Scrap.

targetName: Oregon Waste Systems, Inc. v. Department of Environmental Quality of Ore.
quote: State laws discriminating against interstate commerce on their face are 'virtually per se invalid.' Fulton Corp. v. Faulkner, 516 U. S. 325, 331 (1996) (quoting Oregon Waste Systems, Inc. v. Department of Environmental Quality of Ore., 511 U. S. 93, 99 (1994)).
rationale: The Court cites Oregon Waste Systems as supporting precedent for the principle that facially discriminatory state laws are virtually per se invalid under the Commerce Clause. The citation reinforces rather than criticizes the target case.

quote: In the single case Justice Scalia points to in which we found the per se standard to have been met, Maine v. Taylor, 477 U. S. 131 (1986), the State had no 'reasonable nondiscriminatory alternatives,' Oregon Waste, 511 U. S., at 101 (quoting New Energy Co., 486 U. S., at 278), to the action it had taken. Absent a bar on the import of certain minnows, there was no way for Maine to protect its natural environment from the hazard of parasites and nonnative species that might have been accidentally introduced into the State's waters.
rationale: The Court distinguishes Maine v. Taylor by explaining that in that case Maine had no reasonable nondiscriminatory alternatives to protect its environment, whereas in the present case Maine has ample alternatives to achieve its goal without discriminating against out-of-state campers.

targetName: White v. Massachusetts Council of Construction Employers, Inc.
quote: And in White, the city of Boston had participated in the construction industry by funding certain projects. 460 U. S., at 205-206. These three cases stand for the proposition that, for purposes of analysis under the dormant Commerce Clause, a State acting in its proprietary capacity as a purchaser or seller may 'favor its own citizens over others.'
rationale: The Court cites White as part of its explanation of the market-participant exception to the dormant Commerce Clause. The citation acknowledges and reinforces the precedent rather than criticizing it.

targetName: Board of Education of the Kentucky Annual Conference of the Methodist Episcopal Church v. Illinois
quote: Justice Scalia's heavy reliance upon Board of Ed. of Ky. Annual Conference of Methodist Episcopal Church v. Illinois, 203 U. S. 553 (1906), is misplaced. In that case, a bequest to a Kentucky charitable corporation did not qualify for an exemption from the Illinois inheritance tax because the corporate legatee was not incorporated in Illinois. In this case, the petitioner is a Maine corporation, and the validity of the portion of the Maine statute that denies the exemption to out-of-state corporations is not at issue.
rationale: The Court distinguishes Board of Ed. of Ky. by noting that it involved a different issue (denial of exemption to out-of-state corporations) than the present case, which involves discrimination against in-state corporations serving out-of-state residents.

targetName: Sporhase v. Nebraska Ex Rel. Douglas
quote: We held similarly in Sporhase v. Nebraska ex rel. Douglas, 458 U. S. 941, 958 (1982), that a provision preventing the export of ground water to States not allowing reciprocal export rights was an impermissible barrier to commerce.
rationale: The Court cites Sporhase as supporting precedent for the principle that states cannot discriminate against interstate commerce by restricting exports. The citation reinforces rather than criticizes the target case.

quote: And in Reeves, the State of South Dakota similarly participated in the market for cement as a seller of the output of the cement plant that it had owned and operated for many years. 447 U. S., at 431-432. [...] Maine's tax exemption statute cannot be characterized as a proprietary activity falling within the market-participant exception.
rationale: The Court distinguishes Reeves by explaining that while South Dakota was acting as a market participant in that case by selling cement, Maine's tax exemption cannot be characterized as proprietary activity and thus does not fall within the market-participant exception established in Reeves.

targetName: Walz v. Tax Comm'n of City of New York
quote: In Walz v. Tax Comm'n of City of New York, 397 U. S. 664 (1970), notwithstanding our assumption that a direct subsidy of religious activity would be invalid, we held that New York's tax exemption for church property did not violate the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment. That holding rested, in part, on the premise that there is a constitutionally significant difference between subsidies and tax exemptions.
rationale: The Court distinguishes Walz by noting that while it established a distinction between subsidies and tax exemptions in the Establishment Clause context, this distinction also applies to Commerce Clause analysis, supporting the Court's conclusion that Maine's discriminatory tax exemption is not equivalent to a permissible subsidy.

quote: Because each State was free to adopt measures fostering its own local interests without regard to possible prejudice to nonresidents, what Justice Johnson characterized as a 'conflict of commercial regulations, destructive to the harmony of the States,' ensued. See Gibbons v. Ogden, 9 Wheat. 1, 224 (1824) (opinion concurring in judgment).
rationale: The Court cites Justice Johnson's concurrence in Gibbons v. Ogden to provide historical context for the Commerce Clause. The citation reinforces the importance of the Commerce Clause in preventing discriminatory state regulations.

quote: As our recent cases — particularly Cort v. Ash, 422 U. S. 66 — demonstrate, the fact that a federal statute has been violated and some person harmed does not automatically give rise to a private cause of action in favor of that person.
rationale: The dissent acknowledges Cort v. Ash as an important precedent in determining when to imply a private cause of action, but does not criticize or limit it. Rather, it applies the Cort factors to reach a different conclusion than the majority.

targetName: J. I. Case Co. v. Borak
quote: The question of the existence of a private right of action is basically one of statutory construction. See ante, at 688. And while state courts of general jurisdiction still enforcing the common law as well as statutory law may be less constrained than are federal courts enforcing laws enacted by Congress...
rationale: The dissent distinguishes Borak's more permissive approach to implying private rights of action from the stricter approach now taken by the Court, suggesting that Borak's reasoning should not apply to the current case.

targetName: Allen v. State Board of Elections
quote: The cause of action there recognized— for declaratory relief that a voting change is subject to the authorization requirements of § 5 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, 42 U. S. C. § 1973c — served to trigger the enforcement mechanism provided in the statute itself.
rationale: The dissent distinguishes Allen from the present case by noting that the cause of action in Allen served to trigger an existing statutory enforcement mechanism, whereas the cause of action sought in the current case would displace the enforcement scheme provided in the statute.

quote: In subsequent cases, the Court has continued to give careful attention to claims that a private remedy should be implied in statutes which omit any express remedy. See Santa Clara Pueblo v. Martinez, 436 U. S. 49; Piper v. Chris-Craft Industries, 430 U. S. 1.
rationale: The dissent cites Santa Clara Pueblo as an example of the Court's careful approach to implying private remedies, without criticizing or distinguishing it, but rather using it to support the argument for a stricter approach to implied causes of action.

targetName: Regents of the University of California v. Bakke
quote: I have set out once before my reasons for concluding that a new private cause of action to enforce Title VI should not be implied, University of California Regents v. Bakke, 438 U. S. 265, 379 (1978) (separate opinion of White, J.)
rationale: The dissent cites Justice White's own separate opinion in Bakke to support his consistent position against implying a private cause of action under Title VI, without criticizing the Bakke decision itself.

targetName: National Railroad Passenger Corporation v. National Assn. of Railroad Passengers
quote: True, this Court has sometimes refused to imply private rights of action where administrative or like remedies are expressly available. E.g., National Railroad Passenger Corp. v. National Assn. of Railroad Passengers, 414 U. S. 453; T. I. M. E. Inc. v. United States, 359 U. S. 464.
rationale: The dissent cites National Railroad as supporting the principle that private rights of action should not be implied when administrative remedies are expressly available, using it to bolster the argument against implying a cause of action in the current case.

targetName: Bossier Parish School Board v. Ura Bernard Lemon
quote: However, to the extent the court based its holding on the proposition that an individual protected by a statute always has a right to enforce that statute, it was in error; and an erroneous interpretation of Title VI should not be compounded through importation into Title IX under the guise of effectuating legislative intent.
rationale: The dissent explicitly criticizes the reasoning in Bossier Parish, stating it was in error to the extent it held that individuals protected by a statute automatically have a right to enforce it, and argues against extending this erroneous interpretation to Title IX.
